docs.title: CleanWRT: OpenWrt for the Arcadyan AW1000
docs.text:
CleanWRT is an independent, community build of OpenWrt 25.12.5 for the Arcadyan AW1000 5G router (Qualcomm IPQ8072, Quectel RG500Q-EA modem). It adds AWvoice, which turns the RJ11 socket into a working phone line, a working 5G stack, a modern interface and a curated set of opt-in apps to stock OpenWrt. It is built in the open on GitHub from pinned sources.

If you own an AW1000 and want OpenWrt on it, with a desk phone on the RJ11 socket and a 5G link that reconnects on its own, this is the place to start. The pages below take you from "is my router supported?" to a flashed, working router, and tell you how to get out if something goes wrong.

Not affiliated with OpenWrt

CleanWRT is Powered by OpenWrt and is not affiliated with or endorsed by the OpenWrt project. OpenWrt® is a registered trademark of Software Freedom Conservancy (SFC).

  • Plug in a phone: AWvoice

    Use a normal desk phone on the router's RJ11 socket and make calls over your SIM. No extra box, no PBX, no SIP account. The router's own web page is a telephone too, and works with the socket empty.

    Flash from the stock firmware (UART + TFTP) or from an existing OpenWrt install.

docs.title: What you get on top of stock OpenWrt
docs.text:
• AWvoice, phone calls on the RJ11 port: an ordinary desk phone makes and takes calls over the SIM, with caller id, call waiting, hold, recall of a held call, a call log, call recordings, an answering machine, speed dial, call blocking and alarm calls. Three things can hold the line — the handset, the browser page, and a soft phone on your own network — and the socket can be empty. See the phone port, and its quiet hours.
  • A 5G stack that works out of the box: QModem UI, auto-dial, dual-stack IPv4/IPv6 data, TTL control, SMS, a registration fix for data-only SIMs, per-interface vnStat accounting.
  • A modern interface: the Footstrap theme with dark and light mode, a top bar or a sidebar, five palettes, an accent colour of your choice and a photo or pattern behind the pages.
  • Real front-panel LEDs: a small daemon that shows 5G type, signal quality and internet reachability, with a night mode. See Front-panel LEDs.
  • Proxy and VPN tools: Passwall, Passwall2, HomeProxy, WireGuard, OpenVPN, Tailscale and Cloudflare Tunnel, all installed and all off until you configure them.
  • Opt-in apps: file sharing, DLNA, printer server, Syncthing, AdGuard Home, qBittorrent, Adblock and more. Nothing listens on your network until you tick Enable.
  • Safe defaults: LuCI over HTTPS, BBR congestion control, no open services, no hidden remote access.
  • Verifiable releases: every release has checksums and a provenance bundle (the full build configuration, the pinned sources and the package manifest).

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
What is CleanWRT?

CleanWRT is an independent build of OpenWrt 25.12.5 for the Arcadyan AW1000 5G router. On top of stock OpenWrt it adds a working RJ11 phone port (AWvoice), a 5G modem stack that dials and recovers by itself, the Footstrap theme, front-panel LED management and a set of apps that stay off until you enable them.

Which routers does CleanWRT support?

Only the Arcadyan AW1000 (the Telstra variant) with the expanded flash layout. Never flash it on another router, because an image built for a different partition table can brick the device. See Hardware and MTD layout.

How is CleanWRT different from stock OpenWrt on the AW1000?

It is OpenWrt 25.12.5 with the AW1000 pieces already working: the phone port with VoLTE calls, QModem for the 5G modem, a modern dark and light interface, LEDs that show 5G type and signal quality, and VPN and proxy tools that are installed but off by default.

Is CleanWRT free to use?

Yes. The build configuration, patches and scripts are GPL-2.0-only. The bundled packages keep their own licences, and QModem adds a non-commercial clause, so read Licence and notices before any business use.

docs.title: AWvoice: a phone line on the router
docs.text:
AWvoice turns the AW1000's RJ11 socket into a working telephone line. The call is carried by the router's 5G modem over VoLTE, so your SIM's number is the line's number: no PBX, no Asterisk, no SIP provider, no second number.

Three things can hold that line, and none of them needs the others:

what it is what it does A handset an ordinary analogue phone on the RJ11 socket lifts, dials, rings, shows caller id on its own display The web page the router's own LuCI page a keypad, a call rail, a microphone and a speaker: the browser is the phone A network phone a soft phone on your own LAN registers to the router and rings and dials through the same SIM line

The socket can be empty. With nothing plugged into it, the web page and a soft phone both make and take calls, which is what makes the router usable as a phone without buying a handset for it.

Read this before you connect anything

  • About 46 V DC sits on the RJ11 contacts, and up to about 100 V while a call rings. Do not touch the contacts, and do not wire the socket into anything but a telephone.
  • This is not equipment for emergency calls. The line exists only while the router has power, the modem is registered for VoLTE and your operator carries the call. There is no certification and no battery backup. Keep a phone that works independently for emergencies.
  • Nothing on this router blocks an emergency number, and a dialled emergency number is never replaced by a speed-dial entry. That is a property of the design, not a guarantee of service.

docs.title: What is on when the router boots
docs.text: The phone line on. awvoice.main.enabled ships as 1, so the service starts at boot and the line is ready The web page available as soon as LuCI is; it needs no separate switch The browser's microphone and speaker off until you press the page's audio button, once per browser The network phone side off. Nothing speaks SIP and no SIP port is open until you switch it on Call recordings off The answering machine off, although a greeting ships with the package so it works the moment you switch it on Quiet hours off until you write a window; with no window the phone rings at every hour

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
The packages are already in CleanWRT, so there is nothing to install. Plug an ordinary analogue phone with an RJ11 plug into the socket, and lift the handset: you should hear a dial tone.

If the line was switched off at some point, switch it back on:

uci set awvoice.main.enabled=1
uci commit awvoice
/etc/init.d/awvoice restart

Then, in any order you like:

  1. Open Services → AWvoice(RJ11) and read the page tour beside the real thing.
  2. Make a call from the page's keypad with the handset unplugged, to see that the line does not depend on the socket.
  3. Decide what should happen to a call you do not answer: the answering machine or quiet hours. Joining two calls into one conversation is a separate switch, and it is off as installed.
  4. If a soft phone on your own network should ring too, turn on the SIP side — and read what it opens before you do.

What you need for the line itself: a SIM and an operator that provide VoLTE, and the modem in PCM slave mode. AWvoice reads both, reports them on the Health tab, and never changes the modem's audio mode by itself. The line chip's board file ships with the package and is installed on the first start, so there is nothing to prepare.

docs.title: The page
docs.text:
One LuCI page at Services → AWvoice(RJ11), seven tabs. It reads the daemon over ubus and writes the same /etc/config/awvoice file the shell does, so the page and uci never disagree.

tab what lives there the page that explains it Overview the line's state, the current call, and the browser phone with its keypad and call rail the web page Calls the call log, and each call's own recording or message calls Rules four panes: the phone book, call blocking, alarm calls, quiet hours quiet hours, rules Phone settings the line's behaviour, the tones, the levels, the recording and answering-machine cards the handset, recordings and the machine SIP whether a phone on your own network may join the line, and the account it signs in with network phones Health what the hardware actually reported: rates, guards, storage, the last call's outcome health and tests Test tools the ring test, the line test, and the loopback call test, which this build does not offer yet health and tests

Every control's label, what it writes and when it is disabled is listed in the page tour.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Three packages, and the line logic in one daemon:

package what it is kmod-awvoice-fxs the kernel module: the line chip's register bus, the PCM block, the audio bridge between the modem and the chip, the capture tap that feeds the recordings, the playback ring that carries a greeting and the page's voice to the caller, and the hardware ring watchdog. GPL-2.0-only awvoice-phoned the phone daemon: the hook, the tones, dialling, ringing, caller id, the call log, the recordings, the machine, quiet hours, the page's audio stream, the front end a network phone speaks through, and the ubus service awvoice luci-app-awvoice the LuCI page

The short version of the design: a watchdog, not a promise — if the phone service ever stops, the kernel puts the chip back into reset within milliseconds, so the line cannot be left ringing. Everything else follows from a 20 ms frame that is the unit everywhere, from the kernel bridge to the browser stream to the recording file.

The long version, including the front-end socket, the HD-voice negotiation and the board file, is in how it works.

docs.text: Start with troubleshooting: no dial tone, one-way audio, no caller id, a machine that will not answer, a soft phone that registers but never rings, a browser page with no sound. Each symptom has one check that decides it.

docs.title: Build from source
docs.text: Anyone can rebuild a release. The repository holds only build configuration, patches and the rootfs overlay: no firmware binaries and no package source. Packages are fetched from their upstream feeds at build time, every one pinned to a commit.

docs.title: Repository layout
docs.text:
The firmware repository pins several smaller repositories, listed with their documentation on the Repositories page. This is the layout of the firmware repository itself:

Path What it is configs/arcadyan_aw1000.seed the package selection and image identity configs/local-packages.pin out-of-feed packages, pinned to a commit configs/license-overrides.tsv licences for packages that record none feeds.conf.default every feed, pinned to a commit feeds-src/cwfeed/ the vendored feed (qBittorrent stack, AdGuard Home app, Syncthing app) files/ the rootfs overlay (first-boot scripts, defaults, banner) patches/feeds/ patches applied to the pinned feeds, with zero fuzz patches/tree/ patches applied to files the OpenWrt tree carries itself (packages, build system), with zero fuzz tools/ the build script and its helpers docker/Dockerfile the pinned build environment .github/workflows/ the checks and the build

docs.title: On GitHub Actions
docs.text:
The build needs nothing but the repository.

Workflow When What it does check every push and pull request shell syntax, the version label, that the pins resolve, and a config check: feeds, patches, pins, defconfig and the seed checks, without compiling build by hand (Actions → build → Run workflow) or when a tag v<version> is pushed builds the image in the Docker environment, with a download cache and a compiler cache

The inputs of a manual run:

Input Default Meaning clean off rebuild every package opt_artifacts off also compile and verify the optional cw-opt feed artifacts off upload the images as a workflow artifact (public for a public repository)

A job is limited to six hours by GitHub. A cold build takes roughly two hours; later builds are shorter because of the caches.

A tag v<version> is built by the same workflow, and its images go straight into a draft release: nothing is public and the site is not touched until that draft is published by hand.

docs.title: Locally
docs.text:
You need a Linux machine (or a Linux VM) and Docker.

git clone --depth 1 --branch v25.12.5 https://github.com/openwrt/openwrt.git openwrt
docker build -t cleanwrt-builder docker/
docker run --rm \
  -v "$PWD/openwrt":/build -v "$PWD/cleanwrt-aw1000":/cleanwrt \
  cleanwrt-builder /cleanwrt/tools/cw-release-build.sh /build --clean

The sysupgrade image and a provenance bundle land in openwrt/bin/targets/qualcommax/ipq807x/.

Check first, compile later

CW_CHECK_ONLY=1 runs the feed, patch, pin, defconfig and seed checks and stops before compiling. Pass it with -e CW_CHECK_ONLY=1 to docker run. It takes a few minutes and catches almost every configuration mistake.

docs.title: What the build script guarantees
docs.text:
tools/cw-release-build.sh applies the overlay, the pinned feeds and the patches (to the feeds and to the tree), then runs the mandatory post-defconfig fixups, and it fails rather than ship something stale:

  • the OpenWrt tree must be exactly at v25.12.5;
  • the version label in the seed and in the script must agree;
  • every feed and every local package must match its pinned commit;
  • a feed or tree patch that no longer applies cleanly fails the build, because the upstream code changed;
  • every package the seed selects must survive make defconfig;
  • init scripts must be executable and use procd correctly;
  • the image must fit the flash layout (UBI_PEBS ... line) and the size gate;
  • the kernel modules repository the image points at must have the vermagic of the built kernel;
  • the finished release is verified before it is called OK (tools/cw-check-image.sh): the three images present and non-empty, sha256sums matching the files on disk, the version label and device in the config that was built, the provenance bundle complete, the manifest carrying the selected packages, and the tree signing with the key the devices trust.

docs.title: Signing
docs.text:
Key Purpose How image signing (usign) signs every image tools/cw-sign-keys.sh --generate <tree> creates keys-release/. Never commit it. The build uses it when present. apk key the key every image trusts and the one that signs the optional cw-opt feed one fixed pair: the public half is committed at files/etc/apk/keys/public-key.pem and ships in the overlay; the private half is the repository secret APK_PRIVATE_KEY (and keys-release/private-key.pem for a local release build), never committed. The build writes it to <tree>/private-key.pem, and tools/cw-check-release-keys.sh proves the two halves match.

A tree with no key lets OpenWrt generate one during the build, so every image carried a different /etc/apk/keys/public-key.pem and a device could no longer verify the cw-opt feed built from the same source. The patch in patches/tree/ removes a second build-to-build change: apk mkpkg stamps the build's own clock into every package, because a shallow clone has no per-package git history to take a date from, so /lib/apk/db/installed recorded a different checksum for every package in every image. Running mkpkg with a fixed epoch is the change upstream OpenWrt made; a package's own source date still sets its SourceDateEpoch, and rootfs timestamps are normalised as before, so nothing on the device changes.

On GitHub Actions these keys come from the repository secrets APK_PRIVATE_KEY, USIGN_KEY_BUILD and USIGN_KEY_BUILD_PUB. Without them the images are unsigned and the cw-opt feed stays disabled.

docs.title: What this build changes upstream
docs.text: Every patch this repository applies to someone else's code, and what each one is for. They are applied with patch -p1 at zero fuzz: a patch that does not apply cleanly fails the build rather than shipping a half-applied change.

docs.title: The QModem feed
docs.text: patch what it changes 0002-quectel-cm-ipv6-optional IPv6 gets its own retry ladder — 60 seconds, doubling, capped at 32 minutes — so a failed IPv6 setup no longer tears down the IPv4 call 0003-ndisc6-source-mirror the source mirror, because the original host answers 410 Gone 0004-sip-inbound-answer-delivered an inbound INVITE now carries a transaction-completion callback, so the LAN's 200 OK reaches the answer handler and the 2xx is ACKed as RFC 3261 requires. It also fixes a use-after-free that segfaulted the service 0005-sip-dialog-bye-both-directions the BYE is built as UAC or UAS depending on which side opened the dialog, and an in-dialog BYE is authenticated by the dialog's identity rather than challenged. A hang-up on the cellular side now tears the LAN leg down 0006-sip-cancel-unanswered-lan-invite a LAN INVITE that the handset, the machine or the page took is CANCELed, and the resulting 487 is consumed as the CANCEL's answer instead of being read as a failed call 0007-sip-inbound-credentials-from-uci /etc/config/qmodem_sip becomes the record of the inbound credential, and the runtime file under /var/run is derived from it at start and on reload 0008-sip-default-config-for-the-phone-bridge the defaults this router needs: the media socket pointed at the phone daemon, the inbound direction on, the account named awvoice, the password shared with the Wi-Fi key, and the vendor engine's own path switched off 0009-sip-voip-default-migration a first-boot script that migrates a configuration that still pointed at the vendor engine — and only when the media socket is the phone daemon's, so a hand-configured router is left alone 0010-qmi-wwan-nss-path-behind-its-own-guard restores the vendor-deleted CONFIG_RMNET_DATA guard. Without it modpost fails on a symbol this tree does not carry and the driver cannot be packaged at all

docs.title: The LuCI feed
docs.text: patch what it changes 0001-status-firmware-version-drop-luci-suffix the Firmware Version row shows the release description alone. A detached-HEAD feed was stamping "LuCI (HEAD detached at …)" into a user-facing page 0006-p910nd-menu-title-printer-server the menu title, from p910nd - Printer server to Printer server 0007-upgrade-check-cdn-no-asu the newer-version notice: the wording says CleanWRT, the links point at this project's releases rather than the OpenWrt CDN, and the version feed is pr0luci.github.io/cleanwrt-aw1000/.versions.json 0008-p910nd-mdns-type-label the option label reads mDNS type 0009-filemanager-default-width the file manager's default width, 400 to 800

docs.title: Other feeds, and the OpenWrt tree itself
docs.text: patch what it changes 3ginfo/0002-3ginfo-executable-mode 3ginfo.sh gains its executable bit, because LuCI fs.execs it directly and a fresh boot could fail before the chmod script ran 3ginfo/0003-3ginfo-menu-title the menu title becomes 3gInfo-lite diskman/0001-disk-manager-menu-rename-services-move Disk Manager moves from the System menu to Services, with its title and every internal link passwall_packages/0001-dns2socks-naiveproxy-sources two upstream release assets that no longer exist: dns2socks carries its source in the package, naiveproxy points at a prebuilt version tree/0001-apk-package-timestamps-zero apk mkpkg runs with a fixed epoch, so two builds of one commit produce identical images

docs.title: Themes
docs.text: patch what it changes packages/luci-theme-footstrap/0001-login-page-carries-the-image-logo one line: the login page shows the CleanWRT logo where the theme prints the router's hostname. The image file lives outside the theme's own directory, so a theme update can neither overwrite it nor collide with the patch packages/luci-theme-argon/0001-argon-registers-itself-and-leaves-the-default deletes the line in Argon's first-boot script that made it the default design. An installed theme is offered, not selected

docs.title: Changing a patch or moving a pin
docs.text:
• Move a feed pin: change the commit after the ^ in feeds.conf.default, then make sure every patch in patches/feeds/ still applies (the check workflow does this).
  • Re-port a patch: apply it to the new upstream by hand, regenerate it with diff -u, and keep the header that says what it changes and why.
  • Add a tree patch: put it in patches/tree/, with paths from the tree root (for example include/package-pack.mk). tools/cw-apply-feed-patches.sh reverses the tree patches before every feeds update and applies them again at the start of the build.

docs.title: 25.12.5-R1
docs.text:
The first stable release of the OpenWrt 25.12.5 base. It carries everything 25.12.5-rc2.1 shipped — AWvoice 1.1.3 with the LAN SIP side, the web phone, the code a phone scans and quiet hours, Footstrap as the default look, Alpha and Argon alongside it, the phone bridge's working defaults and the vendor VoIP engine kept off the boot path — and adds two changes:

  • the provenance bundle is verifiable. sha256sums.cw names the bundle's files under cw-release-provenance/, while the release step packed them as provenance/, so the checksums could not be run against the bundle. The bundle now keeps the name the checksums use, and the build unpacks it again and verifies those lines before anything is uploaded.
  • The LED Management picture in the documentation is the page as the released package draws it: the live status strip takes its surface from the active theme and the form is LuCI's own.

docs.title: 25.12.5-rc2.1
docs.text:
• AWvoice 1.1.3 (rc2 shipped 1.1.2). The phone port gains its SIP side. A switch on the new SIP tab starts and stops the LAN SIP service this image now carries, so a soft phone on your own network rings and dials through the SIM's line beside the handset on the RJ11 port; the tab shows the accounts and passwords it uses and what it reports while a call is up. The page also carries a web phone - the handset's audio in the browser - and a code a phone can scan, which writes the account a soft phone fetches into a directory of its own. Wideband voice follows what the modem answers, the caller-id message and the ring supervision were corrected, and the front end now behaves the same in every mode. The same version also carries quiet hours: windows of the day that hold the handset, the answering machine and the network phones off a ringing call, contacts marked to ring through one, and the *78, *79 and # codes on the handset and the page. The vendor's VoIP engine is kept off the boot path (files/etc/uci-defaults/51-cw-awvoice-voipd-off) so the phone daemon itself serves the SIP side.
  • Six patches to that SIP service. Three complete the transaction the cellular side opens: the 2xx ACK a UAC owes, the BYE from either side of a dialog with the in-dialog authentication an in-dialog BYE needs, and the CANCEL of an unanswered LAN INVITE with its 487 recognised. One makes the UCI section the record of the inbound credential, one sets the defaults the phone bridge needs, and one migrates a configuration that kept the VoIP engine's socket (AWvoice).
  • The web interface is Footstrap, an upstream Apache-2.0 LuCI theme pinned to one commit and changed by one line of it - the login page now carries the CleanWRT logo where the theme prints the router's hostname. The LuCI feed now carries a copy of this theme too, at an older commit and under the same package name; the image ships the pinned one, and the build says on every run which package it took out of the feed to do that. The theme that shipped before it is out of the image, with the five feed patches written for it - four that drew card-style status widgets and one that read a CPU counter. The stock Bootstrap theme stays as the fallback and Argon and Alpha ship beside it for comparison, with the one line of Argon's first-boot script that claimed the default removed - an installed theme is offered, not selected. Alpha keeps the Lua template layout it was written for, so its pages are the one thing in this image that may not render as intended on 25.12; choosing it changes nothing else. A new router starts at the look files/etc/uci-defaults/50-cw-footstrap-look writes, with the photo and the pattern that go with it (theme).
  • files/etc/uci-defaults/49-cw-awvoice-provision-port opens the plain HTTP listener that serves the scanned account file, on the LAN only, from a directory that holds nothing else.
  • The QModem feed pin moves to the commit that first carries that SIP service.
  • Terminal moves from the Tools menu to System, and Tools sits where its own order says.

docs.title: 25.12.5-rc2
docs.text:
• AWvoice 1.1.2 (rc1 shipped 1.0.0). The phone port gains call recordings: a call you answer is kept as a stereo WAV, the caller and the handset on separate channels, played, saved or deleted from the call's card. Off by default, with a size budget that removes the oldest.
  • The answering machine: after a delay you set, an unanswered call hears your greeting and leaves a message, played, saved or deleted from the call's card. Off until a greeting is on the router; picking up the handset takes the call over and keeps the part of the message already recorded.
  • Caller id: the message goes out framed, from on-hook transmission between the ring bursts, and the handset shows the national number with the name from your phone book.
  • An upgrade keeps the line: the module loads from the installed package and the daemon checks its interface before it drives the line, instead of running against whatever module the boot had loaded.
  • The three AWvoice packages share one version, 1.1.2.

docs.title: 25.12.5-rc1
docs.text:
First release candidate.

  • OpenWrt 25.12.5 base for the Arcadyan AW1000 (qualcommax/ipq807x, kernel 6.12.94).
  • AWvoice: an ordinary desk phone on the RJ11 port makes and takes calls over the SIM, with caller id, call waiting, hold, three-way join (flash + 3), recall of a held call, call log, speed dial, call blocking, hotline and alarm calls.
  • 5G stack: QModem, vendor QMI dialer, 3ginfo-lite with a registration fix for data-only SIMs, SMS, TTL, vnStat.
  • A dark interface theme with dark and light mode, a sidebar and card-style status widgets.
  • Front-panel LED daemon (power, Wi-Fi, 5G type, signal, internet) with a night mode.
  • Proxy and VPN tools installed and disabled: Passwall, Passwall 2, HomeProxy, WireGuard, OpenVPN, Tailscale, Cloudflare Tunnel.
  • Opt-in apps installed and disabled: file sharing, DLNA, printer server, Syncthing, AdGuard Home, qBittorrent, Adblock, Disk Manager.
  • Built on GitHub Actions in a pinned Docker environment from pinned sources, with checksums and a provenance bundle.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Improvements are welcome: fixes, documentation, test reports and package suggestions.

docs.title: Reporting problems
docs.text:
See Repositories for which repository an issue belongs in.

Open an issue. Include:

  • the CleanWRT version (cat /etc/openwrt_release),
  • what you expected and what happened,
  • the relevant log lines (logread, or the output of cw-diag full).

Never post secrets

Do not paste passwords, Wi-Fi keys, tokens or full IMEI/IMSI/ICCID numbers.

docs.title: Changing the repository
docs.text:
main is protected. The rules:

  1. Every change is a pull request; nobody pushes to main directly.
  2. The checks must pass before a pull request can be merged.
  3. Pull requests are merged with squash merge, and the branch is deleted afterwards.
git clone https://github.com/Pr0Luci/cleanwrt-aw1000.git
cd cleanwrt-aw1000
git checkout -b my-change
# edit, then:
git commit -am "Short description of the change"
git push -u origin my-change

Then open a pull request on GitHub.

docs.title: Writing docs
docs.text:
The documentation is the docs/ folder, built with MkDocs Material. Every page has an Edit this page button that opens the right file on GitHub.

pip install mkdocs-material
mkdocs serve        # preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000

The package list page is generated from the build seed; do not edit it by hand.

docs.title: Rules for changes to the firmware
docs.text:
• Keep the overlay small. A new file in files/ ships on every router.
  • A new feed patch must apply with zero fuzz to the pinned commit. Say in its header what it changes and why.
  • Anything that adds a listening service must ship disabled.
  • Do not add translations or internal wording. Keep comments plain and short.
  • Do not commit keys. keys-release/ and private-key.pem are ignored for a reason.

docs.title: From the official repositories
docs.text:
The official OpenWrt 25.12.5 repositories are enabled on every router:

apk update
apk add <package>

Examples that are not part of the image: mwan3 and luci-app-mwan3 (multi-WAN), transmission-daemon (another download client), aria2, luci-app-acme (certificates).

Packages you add yourself stay unpinned and are yours to manage.

docs.title: The optional CleanWRT feed (cw-opt)
docs.text:
CleanWRT can publish its own signed apk feed for packages the official repositories do not carry, such as OpenClash. The feed is not active in the 25.12.5-R1 image: the repository holds a disabled template, files/etc/apk/repositories.d/cw-opt.list.disabled, and the feed is switched on only when its index is published and its signing key exists.

How it is enabled (for the project, not for users):

  1. Build once so the tree creates its apk signing key.
  2. Copy the public half to files/etc/apk/keys/public-key.pem.
  3. Publish the index first. An image that carries a dead feed entry breaks apk update on every device.
  4. Rename the file to cw-opt.list and rebuild.

Until then, apk update talks to the official repositories only, and it works from the first boot.

docs.title: What is already baked in
docs.text: qBittorrent and AdGuard Home are part of the image, with the Qt6 stack that qBittorrent needs. They come from the project's vendored feed (feeds-src/cwfeed) and stay disabled until you enable them.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• Only the Arcadyan AW1000, and only with the expanded flash layout. See MTD layout.
  • The first install from the stock firmware needs a serial console.
  • QModem is not free for commercial use. Its licence adds a non-commercial clause. See Licence and notices.
  • AWvoice is not for emergency calls. See the safety notes on the AWvoice page.
  • Images are unsigned unless the project's image-signing key is configured for the release.
  • The cw-opt package feed is not active yet.
  • The modem's own firmware is separate and is not provided by this project.
  • The phone line is on as installed, because a phone that does not ring is the failure people notice first. Everything else that makes noise — recordings, the answering machine, quiet hours, the network phone side — is off until you switch it on.
  • The three-way join is off as installed. It is its own switch, conference, in Phone settings → Features.
  • The browser phone needs HTTPS and one certificate acceptance. A browser takes no microphone from a page it does not trust, and the audio arrives on a second port.
  • Quiet hours and alarm calls trust the clock. With an untrusted clock no schedule is honoured; a quiet asked for by hand with *78 needs no clock at all.
  • The loopback test call is not offered by this build. The card is there, disabled, and says so.
  • The outbound SIP direction ships with no server, no realm and no password. The direction that reaches outside your house starts empty.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Does OpenWrt run on the Arcadyan AW1000?

Yes. CleanWRT is OpenWrt 25.12.5 built for the AW1000 (qualcommax/ipq807x), with the 5G modem, Wi-Fi, the front-panel LEDs and the RJ11 phone port working. It needs the expanded flash layout, see the MTD layout page.

Can I use a normal phone on the AW1000's RJ11 port?

Yes, with AWvoice, which is part of CleanWRT: an ordinary analogue phone makes and takes calls over the SIM. See the handset.

Does the phone work with nothing plugged into the RJ11 socket?

Yes. The AWvoice page is a telephone — keypad, call rail, flash key, microphone — and a soft phone on your own network can join the same line. See the web phone and network phones.

Can I record calls, and where do the files go?

If you switch recording on. Each answered call is kept on the router as a stereo WAV in /etc/awvoice/recordings/, with a size budget that removes the oldest, and it is played from that call's card in the log. Nothing leaves the router, and no file name carries a number. Check what recording rules apply where you live. See recordings and the machine.

Can the phone stay quiet at night?

Yes: up to eight windows, each silent, sent to the answering machine, or rejecting the caller, with numbers that ring through regardless and *78 / *79 from the handset or the page. See quiet hours.

Why does the browser page not give me a microphone?

Two reasons and both are the browser's rule, not a fault: the page must be open over HTTPS, and the audio stream arrives on its own port whose certificate your browser has not seen. The page has one button for that step, and it stays out of the way afterwards. See the web phone.

Does the AW1000 do VoLTE voice calls on OpenWrt?

Yes, with AWvoice. The 5G modem carries the call over VoLTE, so you need a SIM and an operator that provide VoLTE.

Why does the browser say the connection is not secure?

LuCI uses a self-signed certificate created on your router at first boot. The connection is encrypted, but no public authority signed the certificate. See Security.

I cannot log in after flashing.

The first login is over Ethernet with no password, at http://192.168.1.1. Connect a computer to a LAN port and set its address to 192.168.1.x if it does not get one. If it still fails, use failsafe mode.

Can I flash it on my router if it is not an AW1000?

No. Never flash an image built for another device. It can brick the router.

sysupgrade says the image is not valid.

Check the file name (arcadyan_aw1000), re-download the image and check its checksum. If you flash a community build that has no metadata, you would need -F; do not force an image you did not verify.

The 5G modem does not register.

Open Modem → QModem and Modem → 3gInfo-lite and check the SIM, the APN and the signal. See The 5G modem. A modem firmware upgrade is only a last resort.

The 5G and signal LEDs went dark.

The LED daemon cannot read the modem. Check that nothing holds the AT port open, and read logread -e cw-led. See Front-panel LEDs.

Wi-Fi works but 'Internet' says unreachable.

Open the connectivity check settings in System → LED Management. The LED only mirrors the probe. Test the real connection from a computer too.

Cloudflared shows a red error.

That is expected until you configure the tunnel token. See Remote access.

I ran apk upgrade and the overview cards look different.

The LuCI packages are pinned for a reason (see Updating and pinning). Flash the release again to get back to its state. A factory reset does not restore replaced packages.

Downloads are filling the router's flash.

Downloads default to the first USB drive. Plug a drive in before you start a download.

Can I use it commercially?

The project is free of charge. The bundled QModem component prohibits commercial use. Check its licence before you deploy this firmware in a business, an ISP or a paid service.

How do I go back to the stock firmware?

Restoring the stock firmware needs the stock image and a serial console. Keep a backup of the stock firmware before you flash.

What is the default IP address and login of CleanWRT on the AW1000?

The router answers at http://192.168.1.1 over Ethernet, with no root password at first. LuCI asks you to set one. Wi-Fi starts as CleanWRT-5G and CleanWRT-2.4G with the default key CleanWRT#40, so change it on the first login.

Do I need a serial cable to install OpenWrt on the AW1000?

For the first install from the stock firmware, yes: a 3.3 V USB-UART adapter and a TFTP server. If the router already runs OpenWrt, you can update with sysupgrade or from LuCI with no cable. See Installation.

Where do I download the AW1000 firmware, and how do I verify it?

On the GitHub Releases page of the project. Check the file with sha256sum -c sha256sums.cw --ignore-missing before you flash, and make sure the file name contains arcadyan_aw1000. See Releases.

How do I recover an AW1000 that will not boot?

If the router boots but you cannot reach it, use failsafe mode over Ethernet. If it is stuck at the bootloader, use the serial console to boot an initramfs image over TFTP and flash again. See Recovery.

docs.title: Still stuck?
docs.text:
1. Collect a diagnostic capture: cw-diag full (SIM identifiers, public IPs and Wi-Fi keys are redacted).
  2. Read the Recovery page.
  3. Open an issue on GitHub with the version, what you did, and the relevant log lines. Do not paste passwords or keys.

docs.title: First boot
docs.text: CleanWRT follows the stock OpenWrt first-login model.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
Address 192.168.1.1 Hostname CleanWRT Root password none (set it on first login) Wi-Fi on, WPA2-PSK, networks CleanWRT-2.4G, CleanWRT-5G (and CleanWRT-6G on a 6 GHz radio) Default Wi-Fi key CleanWRT#40 Time zone UTC (set yours in LuCI) Admin UI LuCI over HTTPS (self-signed certificate) The phone line on. awvoice.main.enabled ships as 1, so a desk phone works the first time you plug one in The network phone (SIP) side off. No SIP port is open and no SIP process runs until the AWvoice page's switch starts it The front-panel LED daemon on The TTL rewrite for tethering on, at 64 Opt-in apps installed and off, with one exception: the Samba daemon starts, but its share allows no guest access, so nothing is reachable until you add users

Change both on the first login

Anyone who knows the default Wi-Fi key can join your network, and with no root password anyone on the LAN can log in. Do the steps below before you connect the router to anything you do not trust.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Connect a computer to a LAN port with Ethernet. Do not use Wi-Fi for the first login.
  2. Open http://192.168.1.1. The browser is moved to HTTPS and shows a certificate warning. That is expected, see Security.
  3. LuCI asks you to set a root password. Set a strong one. It applies to LuCI and SSH.

  4. Change the Wi-Fi key: Network → Wireless, edit each interface, Wireless Security.

    uci set wireless.default_radio0.key='your-strong-key'
uci set wireless.default_radio1.key='your-strong-key'
uci commit wireless && wifi reload

  5. Set your time zone: System → System → General Settings.

  6. Open Modem and check that the 5G modem registered. See The 5G modem.

The root password is set under System → Administration:

Upgrades with keep settings never overwrite a key you have set yourself.

The login page, in dark and light mode:

Dark Light

docs.text: Every opt-in app has the same single switch: open its LuCI page, tick Enable, press Save & Apply. Set any passwords the app needs before you enable it. See What is included.

docs.title: What the image did before you got here
docs.text: Thirteen first-boot scripts wrote the defaults above — the hostname, the SSIDs and the key, the HTTPS redirect, the theme's look, the LED ownership, the AT port handed to the phone service, the vendor VoIP engine taken off the boot path, and the package pins that keep apk upgrade from replacing patched LuCI packages. All of it, script by script and option by option, is in first-boot defaults.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
CleanWRT supports one device: the Arcadyan AW1000 5G router (the Telstra variant).

No other device

Flashing this image on any other router can brick it. The partition table lives on the router, not in the image, and an image built for a different table is the classic way to destroy a router.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
SoC Qualcomm IPQ8072 (ipq807x), four cores Memory 1 GiB RAM, 1 GiB NAND flash 5G modem Quectel RG500Q-EA (separate firmware, see The 5G modem) Wi-Fi Qualcomm ath11k radios Ethernet Qualcomm NSS data plane Kernel Linux 6.12.94 Target qualcommax/ipq807x, board name arcadyan,aw1000 OpenWrt base 25.12.5

The official OpenWrt Table of Hardware page has further background on the device.

docs.title: Front panel
docs.text: The router has indicator LEDs for power, Wi-Fi, 5G, signal, internet and phone. CleanWRT drives the first five; see Front-panel LEDs. The phone LED belongs to AWvoice and is left alone by the LED app.

docs.title: The phone port
docs.text: The AW1000 has an RJ11 socket with a line-interface chip, for an ordinary analogue phone. AWvoice uses it to make and take calls over the SIM card. Mind the voltages on the contacts, and see the safety notes on that page.

docs.title: What you need to know before flashing
docs.text:
• The router must have the expanded flash layout. The stock layout is too small. See MTD layout.
  • The first install from the stock firmware needs a serial console. See the UART guide.
  • Keep a copy of the stock firmware settings if you may ever want to go back.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
What chip and memory does the Arcadyan AW1000 have?

A Qualcomm IPQ8072 with four cores, 1 GiB of RAM and 1 GiB of NAND flash. Wi-Fi comes from Qualcomm ath11k radios, and the Ethernet ports sit on the NSS data plane.

Which 5G modem is inside the Arcadyan AW1000?

A Quectel RG500Q-EA. Its firmware is separate from the router firmware, so flashing CleanWRT does not touch it. See The 5G modem.

Which AW1000 does CleanWRT run on?

The Arcadyan AW1000 in its Telstra variant, and nothing else. The image is built for board arcadyan,aw1000 on qualcommax/ipq807x, and an image for a different partition table can brick a router.

Does the Arcadyan AW1000 have a phone port?

Yes. It has an RJ11 socket with a line-interface chip. With AWvoice an ordinary analogue desk phone can make and take calls over the SIM card.

docs.title: IPv6 and proxies
docs.text: The 5G connection is dual-stack when your carrier offers IPv6. If you send traffic through Passwall 2, enable IPv6 TProxy in its forwarding settings. To use IPv4 only, set the modem's PDP type to IPv4 in Modem → QModem.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Read this page fully before you start

Supported hardware is the Arcadyan AW1000 only. Flashing the wrong image or flashing on the wrong flash layout can brick the router. Read MTD layout and Recovery before you flash.

There are two situations:

  1. The router already runs OpenWrt (stock OpenWrt 25.12.x or an earlier CleanWRT). Go to Already on OpenWrt.
  2. The router runs the stock (Telstra) firmware. The first OpenWrt install needs serial console (UART) access. Go to First install from stock.

docs.title: What you need for a first install
docs.text:
• A 3.3 V USB-UART adapter. Do not use 5 V logic. Plus a few wires.
  • A Phillips screwdriver to open the case, and a look at the UART guide to find the pads.
  • A TFTP server on your computer (atftpd, tftpd-hpa, or dnsmasq --enable-tftp) with a fixed IP in the router's LAN range (factory default 192.168.1.x).
  • Two files from a release (see Releases):
    • …-initramfs-uImage.itb, the boot-in-RAM image for the first install
    • …-squashfs-sysupgrade.bin, the permanent image
  • An Ethernet cable. The first login is over Ethernet.

docs.title: First install from stock firmware (UART + TFTP)
docs.text:
1. Open the case, connect the UART adapter (3.3 V!) and open a serial terminal at 115200 8N1 (screen /dev/ttyUSB0 115200, or PuTTY).
  2. Power the router on and interrupt U-Boot when the countdown appears (press a key).

  3. Tell U-Boot the router's IP and your TFTP server's IP:

    setenv ipaddr 192.168.1.1
setenv serverip 192.168.1.10   # your computer running TFTP

  4. Boot the initramfs image from RAM:

    tftpboot ${loadaddr} <initramfs-image-name>.itb
bootm ${loadaddr}

  5. The router boots a live OpenWrt from RAM. Flash the permanent image from this live system, over the network:

    # from your computer
scp *-squashfs-sysupgrade.bin root@192.168.1.1:/tmp/
# on the router
sysupgrade -v /tmp/*-squashfs-sysupgrade.bin

  6. The router reboots into the permanent firmware. Continue with First boot.

The no-UART shortcut

On very old stock firmware revisions a community "autoscript" method exists (flashing via a crafted USB update file, no UART). It is not maintained here, the older methods are reported to be patched on newer stock firmware, and a wrong image for your flash layout can brick the device. Prefer UART + TFTP.

docs.title: Already on OpenWrt (sysupgrade)
docs.text:
scp *-arcadyan_aw1000-squashfs-sysupgrade.bin root@192.168.1.1:/tmp/
ssh root@192.168.1.1 "sysupgrade -v /tmp/*-sysupgrade.bin"
  • Keep settings (the default): your configuration survives. This is fine between CleanWRT releases.
  • Clean install (sysupgrade -n): wipes the overlay. Use it when changing major versions, when the UI misbehaves, or when coming from a much older build. It also puts the default credentials back (see First boot).

You can also upload the image in LuCI, under System → Backup / Flash Firmware → Flash image….

Before flashing from OpenWrt, check the layout:

cat /proc/mtd

The rootfs partition must be at least 0x08000000 (128 MiB). Otherwise stop. See MTD layout.

docs.title: After flashing
docs.text:
• Open http://192.168.1.1 over Ethernet and follow First boot.
  • Check the version in the login banner or Status → Overview.
  • If something is wrong, go to Recovery.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
How do I install OpenWrt on the Arcadyan AW1000 for the first time?

From the stock firmware you need a 3.3 V USB-UART adapter and a TFTP server. Stop U-Boot on the serial console, boot the initramfs image from RAM over TFTP, then run sysupgrade from that live system to write the permanent image.

Can I install OpenWrt on the AW1000 without opening the case?

If the router already runs OpenWrt, yes: copy the sysupgrade image over and flash it, or use System → Backup / Flash Firmware in LuCI. From the stock firmware you need the serial console. A community no-UART method existed for very old stock firmware, but it is not maintained here and is reported to be patched on newer revisions.

Which file do I flash on the AW1000, initramfs or sysupgrade?

Both, in order, on a first install. The initramfs image only boots a live system from RAM and writes nothing. The sysupgrade image is the permanent one. Later updates need only the sysupgrade image.

Should I keep settings or use sysupgrade -n on the AW1000?

Keep settings between CleanWRT releases. Use sysupgrade -n (a clean install) when you change major versions, when you come from another firmware, or when the interface misbehaves. It also puts the default credentials back.

docs.title: Front-panel LEDs
docs.text:
CleanWRT replaces the stock LED Configuration page with LED Management (System → LED Management), backed by one small daemon, cw-led-daemon. The package is luci-app-cw-led, pinned in this build to one commit.

The LEDs on this board are on or off: there is no dimming anywhere in the hardware, so every state you see is a lit lamp, an unlit lamp, or a blink.

docs.title: The status card
docs.text:
The top of the page shows what the panel is doing right now, refreshed every five seconds, so you can watch the router's state without walking to it.

DarkLightOn a phone

Two chips above the lamps say whether the daemon is running and whether the night window is open. Six tiles show the lamps. The sixth, Phone, is read-only: this app reports what the phone service owns but never writes it.

About the screenshots

These were taken from a real AW1000 running this firmware. The states in them belong to the moment they were taken.

docs.title: What each LED shows
docs.text:
LED Shows Power always on Wi-Fi on while any radio is up. In Single interface mode it blinks with traffic on the interface you choose 5G the 5G type only: solid blue = 5G standalone (SA), solid green = 5G non-standalone (NSA), off for anything else — 4G, 3G, no service, unknown. There is no red on this lamp. While the very first modem read is still running it flashes red at 1 Hz Signal green good, blue average, red poor; flashing red while the modem is searching or the SIM has a fault; off when the service is unavailable Internet on while the connectivity check says the uplink really reaches the internet Phone not this app's lamp. While AWvoice is running it is solid while the line is ready, blinks fast while a call rings and blinks slowly while the handset is off hook

The WAN ethernet port's own lamp is left exactly as the kernel drives it.

docs.title: How signal quality is decided
docs.text:
Signal uses RSRP in dBm, with CSQ as a fallback when RSRP does not come back. The four limits are settings.

excellent (green) poor (red) in between (blue) RSRP at or above -95 at or below -110 between the two CSQ at or above 20 at or below 9 between the two

The page draws the scale (−44 to −140) so you can see where your reading sits, and refuses a pair where the poor threshold is not below the excellent one.

docs.title: How the 5G type is read
docs.text: One AT command answers the question: AT+QENG="servingcell". A NR5G-SA line is standalone, a NR5G-NSA line is non-standalone, LTE or a 3G line is not 5G, and a reply that names no cell at all leaves the lamp off. AT+CSQ is asked only when the serving-cell reply carried no usable RSRP, and AT+CEREG? and AT+CPIN? only while the modem is not registered — fewer queries on a port other programs also use.

docs.title: How the internet LED is decided
docs.text:
Active connectivity probe (HTTP 204) is the default and the most accurate: the daemon asks a test address for an empty 204 answer, and anything else — a captive-portal page, a redirect, a timeout — means there is no internet. That catches the case where the link is up but nothing is reachable, which a link-state check cannot see.

  • One good probe turns the lamp on at once. Two failed probes in a row are needed to turn it off, so one dropped probe does not flicker it. Both numbers are settings.
  • The probe follows the default route and is not bound to one device, so it still works behind a transparent proxy on this router.
  • The plain http:// in the default addresses is deliberate: a captive portal answers an HTTPS request with a certificate error and tells you nothing.
  • On this device the internet lamp reflects the modem data path, not an ethernet WAN.

The other two modes are Default-route interface is up, which is link state only, and Ping a host, which defaults to 1.1.1.1.

docs.title: Night mode
docs.text:
Night mode switches the lamps you choose off between two times of day.

setting default Enabled off Window 22:30 to 06:00. A window that runs past midnight is normal, not an error Keep on during night all five daemon-owned lamps are on the list, so nothing goes dark until you remove one

The page draws the window as a timeline so you can see it, and hides the window controls entirely until night mode is enabled. Entering the window forces every non-exempt lamp off; leaving it re-reads the modem and re-probes at once, so the panel is current again the minute the window closes.

The phone lamp is not in the night list

Night mode here does not touch the phone lamp, and it is not bound to the theme's night behaviour either. A line that must stay silent at night is a quiet hours question, which is answered on the phone's own page.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Everything is on the page and stored in /etc/config/cw-led.

section option on the page as default meaning General enabled Enable LED daemon 1 run the daemon at all General poll_interval Modem poll interval (s) 30 seconds between modem polls. A slider from 10 to 300 General tick — 5 the daemon's own clock in seconds. Everything timed in ticks is measured against it General log_heartbeat_min — 0 write a status line this often; 0 is silent Modem AT port port AT port device /dev/ttyUSB2 the AT port the daemon reads. Saving the page applies and reloads the daemon in one action. Editing the file by hand needs both steps:

/etc/init.d/cw-led reload

docs.title: Under the hood
docs.text:
The daemon is plain shell over the modem's AT port, so it needs no other app and no ubus service of its own. It holds a lock file while it talks on the port, and because a lock cannot bind software that does not know about it, the poll rate stays low by default.

Writes go through sysfs and only when something changes. The daemon compares the live trigger and brightness rather than a cached copy, so a write from anywhere else — an old colour left behind by a crash, a state replay at boot — is corrected within one tick. When the daemon stops it restores the static triggers and parks the lamps it owned.

The first-boot script for this package removes the kernel LED sections that the daemon owns from /etc/config/system, so the stock LED page and this daemon cannot both drive the same lamp. green:power, green:wifi and the WAN port lamp keep their kernel triggers, and green:phone is never read, written or parked by this app.

docs.title: If a lamp looks wrong
docs.text:
Read the log

Every change of the 5G or signal colour is logged with the modem state behind it:

logread -e cw-led
symptom what it means 5G and signal lamps are both off the modem is unreachable on its AT port. Check the port setting, and whether anything else holds it open Lamps flicker or blank for a moment another program is reading the same port. The default ttyUSB2 exists so QModem, on ttyUSB3, does not share it; the grace setting absorbs a cut-short reply Signal is off but the modem is registered the reply carried neither RSRP nor CSQ. The grace holds the last colour for two polls, then blanks it — that blank is honest, not a fault 5G lamp off on a 4G connection correct: the lamp shows 5G only. Nothing is wrong Internet lamp off though the internet works the probe address is blocked. Change Probe URL, or switch to Default-route interface is up Wi-Fi lamp off with the radios up you are in Single interface mode and it is following one interface. Use Auto The lamps went wrong after a reboot the daemon starts early, before the modem has answered anything, so the first few seconds show a red 5G flash. That is the search state, not a fault

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
What do the front-panel LEDs of the Arcadyan AW1000 mean?

Power is always on. Wi-Fi is on while a radio is up. The 5G lamp shows the 5G type: solid blue for standalone, solid green for non-standalone, off for anything else. Signal is green, blue or red for good, average or poor. Internet is on while a real connectivity check passes. Phone belongs to the phone service and is shown here read-only.

How do I turn off the AW1000 LEDs at night?

Enable night mode in System → LED Management. The default window is 22:30 to 06:00 and a window past midnight works. Remove a lamp from the keep-on list to switch it off inside the window. The hardware cannot dim, so a lamp is either off or on.

Why is the 5G LED on my AW1000 off?

It lights for 5G only: off on 4G, 3G, no service, or an unknown type. If the signal lamp is off too, the daemon probably cannot read the modem on its AT port — logread -e cw-led says which.

Why is the internet LED off when my internet works?

The lamp mirrors a probe, not your traffic. If the probe address is blocked it stays off. Change the probe URL, or switch the check to the default-route mode.

Does the LED daemon use the modem's data connection?

No. It reads the modem over an AT port with plain commands and writes lamps through sysfs. It stops working if that port is busy, which is why it is on a different port from QModem.

docs.title: The 5G modem
docs.text: The AW1000 carries a Quectel RG500Q-EA 5G modem. CleanWRT drives it with QModem and the vendor QMI dialer, so it dials and recovers on its own.

docs.title: What works out of the box
docs.text:
feature where notes modem control and status Modem → QModem auto-dial, auto-recovery, dual-stack IPv4/IPv6 when your carrier offers IPv6 signal and network details Modem → 3gInfo-lite registration shows correctly on data-only SIMs, from a CEREG-based fix in this build SMS Modem → SMS read and send. Received messages can be forwarded tethering-detection bypass (TTL) Modem → TTL on by default: forwarded packets get a fixed TTL of 64 data usage Statistics → vnStat daily and monthly totals on the modem interface Wi-Fi regulatory domain automatic taken from the network's country code once the modem registers the LAN SIP service no page of its own — the switch is on AWvoice → SIP it comes with the same feed as the modem apps. See below

About the TTL setting

The TTL rule exists so tethered traffic looks like traffic from the router itself. Whether that is allowed depends on your carrier's terms. Change the value or switch it off in Modem → TTL — the shipped rule is an /etc/nftables.d/ fragment, which is what fw4 actually applies.

docs.title: AWvoice and the modem
docs.text: AWvoice uses this modem for voice, over VoLTE, and needs it in PCM slave mode. If you use the phone port, read that page before you change the modem's audio or IMS settings: AWvoice reads the audio mode and the IMS registration and reports both, and does not change either one itself. Changing the audio rate does restart the modem, so mobile data drops for about half a minute.

docs.title: The SIP service that arrives with this feed
docs.text:
The QModem feed this build pins carries qmodem-sipd, the LAN SIP service that a network phone uses. It is selected into the image, and it is not started by the image.

fact value package qmodem-sipd, which pulls the vendor VoIP engine, the SMS daemon and the seven pjproject libraries size in the image 166 KiB for the service itself, about 1.5 MiB for the seven pjsip packages together config file /etc/config/qmodem_sip, listed option by option in UCI options what starts it the AWvoice page's SIP switch, through /etc/init.d/qmodem_voip_sipd boot order, if enabled SMS daemon 92, phone daemon 95, VoIP engine 99, SIP service 100 what is deliberately not selected luci-app-qmodem-voip. Two pages for one service drift apart, so the switch, the credentials and the audio socket live on the AWvoice screen the vendor VoIP engine stopped and taken off the boot path at first boot, because it claims the front-end name the phone daemon answers

Six patches in patches/feeds/qmodem/ change this service's behaviour — the 2xx ACK, the in-dialog BYE from either side, the CANCEL of an unanswered LAN INVITE, the UCI section as the credential record, the defaults the phone bridge needs, and the migration for a configuration that kept the vendor engine's socket. What each one does is in what this build changes upstream.

If a soft phone registers but no call goes through

That is the vendor VoIP engine holding the front-end name. This image's first-boot script takes it off the boot path for exactly this reason; on a router where the script did not run, the AWvoice page's Diagnostics pane names the holder.

docs.title: IPv4 only
docs.text: To use IPv4 only, set the modem's PDP type to IPv4 in Modem → QModem. If you send traffic through Passwall 2, also enable IPv6 TProxy in its forwarding settings, otherwise devices can reach IPv6 sites directly, outside the proxy.

docs.title: AT ports
docs.text:
The modem exposes several serial ports, and more than one program uses them.

who which port how it is chosen the phone daemon the tty on the modem's USB interface 2 (awvoice.main.at_interface) by interface number, through sysfs — not by a fixed device name the LED daemon /dev/ttyUSB2, configurable by device name. Usually the same port as above, which is why it holds a lock, polls every 30 seconds, and absorbs a cut-short reply with its contention grace setting QModem /dev/ttyUSB3 the port left to it by 47-cw-awvoice-at-port, which removes the ubus AT daemon's claim on the other one

Do not keep a port open

Two programs reading one AT port interleave their replies. A terminal left open on any of them can blank the LEDs, stall QModem, or make the phone daemon's modem questions time out. Close the session when you are done.

A read that does not disturb anything:

( timeout 3 cat /dev/ttyUSB3 > /tmp/at.out & ); sleep 1; printf 'ATI\r' > /dev/ttyUSB3; sleep 2
tr -d '\r' < /tmp/at.out; rm -f /tmp/at.out

ATI      ->  Quectel / RG500Q-EA / Revision: RG500QEAAAR13A01M4G
AT+QGMR  ->  RG500QEAAAR13A01M4G_01.200.01.200

docs.title: Modem firmware
docs.text: The modem's firmware is separate from the router firmware. Flashing CleanWRT does not change it. CleanWRT does not ship, host or redistribute Quectel firmware or tools, and the project has not performed the upgrade itself: it is the vendor's procedure and your risk.

docs.title: When is an upgrade needed?
docs.text: Only when the modem misbehaves on your carrier — no registration, no 5G, unstable data — and the carrier or Quectel confirms that a newer firmware fixes it. Some units are reported to ship with a region-customised firmware that works poorly on other carriers; the revision string above is what to quote when asking Quectel. If the modem works, leave it alone.

docs.title: Where the firmware comes from
docs.text: Only from Quectel, or your supplier acting for Quectel: the package for your exact module variant and revision, with the vendor's release notes. Do not use packages from forums or other sites. A wrong or modified package can brick the modem.

docs.title: The upgrade, in outline
docs.text:
Quectel's Linux flashing tool is QFirehose. It is not in the OpenWrt 25.12.5 package feeds and not in the CleanWRT feed; it comes with the vendor's Linux tools package. Follow the README of the version you receive, because the flags differ between versions.

  1. Read the version and keep the output.
  2. Power the router from a stable supply and do not touch it during the flash.

  3. Stop what uses the modem ports:

    /etc/init.d/cw-led stop
/etc/init.d/awvoice stop
/etc/init.d/qmodem_network stop
/etc/init.d/qmodem_monitor stop

  4. Run QFirehose against the unpacked vendor firmware directory, as its README says.

  5. Wait for the modem to re-enumerate, read the version again, then start the services again — or reboot.

docs.title: Risk and recovery
docs.text:
• An interrupted or wrong flash can leave the modem unusable. A downgrade is not guaranteed to work: plan as if the upgrade is one-way.
  • The router itself is unaffected, so SSH and LuCI stay reachable over LAN and Wi-Fi.
  • If the modem does not come back, the vendor's tool and package are the recovery path.

docs.title: What the image fixes around the modem
docs.text: change why 98-cw-modem-fix enables a small init script a registration fix for data-only SIMs, which otherwise show as not registered 97-cw-net-tuning sets network.globals.packet_steering='1' receive work spread over the four cores, which a 5G link actually uses IPv6 gets its own retry ladder in quectel-CM-5G-M a failed IPv6 setup no longer tears down the IPv4 call. 60 seconds, doubling, capped at 32 minutes qmi_wwan_q keeps its NSS branch behind its own guard without it the module cannot even be packaged in this tree the generic QMI driver is not selected with it the modem registers and gets an address but no data flows. The vendor-patched drivers are what work

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
Why does the 5G modem of my AW1000 not register?

Open Modem → QModem and Modem → 3gInfo-lite and check the SIM, the APN and the signal first. A modem firmware upgrade is a last resort, and only when the carrier or Quectel confirms a newer firmware fixes your case.

How do I read and send SMS on the Arcadyan AW1000?

Modem → SMS in LuCI. Received messages can be forwarded from the same place. Note that this image selects one SMS forwarder deliberately: the two packages that exist install the same init script and the image would refuse to assemble with both.

What does the TTL setting do on the AW1000?

It gives forwarded packets a fixed TTL of 64 so tethered traffic looks like traffic from the router itself. It is on by default. Whether that is allowed depends on your carrier's terms.

Which AT port do I use on the AW1000 modem?

/dev/ttyUSB3 for QModem, and the tty on USB interface 2 for the phone daemon; the LED daemon is configured for /dev/ttyUSB2. Do not leave a terminal open on any of them.

Does CleanWRT include a SIP server?

It includes a LAN SIP service, from the same feed as the modem apps, that a soft phone on your own network registers to. It ships stopped, it listens on nothing until the AWvoice page's switch starts it, and it never reaches outside your network unless you configure the outbound direction yourself.

docs.title: MTD layout
docs.text:
Read this before the first flash

CleanWRT does not fit the stock flash layout of the AW1000. It needs the expanded layout. Flashing it on a stock layout can leave the router unbootable (UART + TFTP recovery needed).

docs.title: What actually has to fit
docs.text:
What must fit is the set of UBI volumes inside the rootfs MTD partition, not the size of the sysupgrade file.

A stock-layout AW1000 has a 100 MiB rootfs partition (0x06400000, which is 400 erase blocks of 256 KiB). UBI reserves part of it for itself:

Reserved by UBI Blocks layout volume 2 wear leveling and erase-block bookkeeping 2 bad-block reserve (20/1024 of the whole 1 GiB chip, whatever the partition size) 80

So 316 blocks (about 76 MiB) are left for volumes. The stock firmware's own UBI on that partition uses exactly 316 (kernel 24 + rootfs 177 + rootfs_data 115).

docs.title: What CleanWRT needs
docs.text:
The 25.12.5-R1 image needs 514 blocks. The published 25.12.5-rc2.1 image measured the same 514 and 25.12.5-rc2 needed 498; R1 carries rc2.1's package set unchanged, so it needs what rc2.1 needed. That is more than the stock layout offers (316) and fits the expanded layout (2720 blocks on a router with a 701 MiB rootfs). The release build prints a line like this and fails if the image does not fit the layout it targets:

UBI_PEBS volumes need 514 PEBs; stock 100 MiB layout (316): does NOT fit; gate layout=expanded (capacity 2720)

A sysupgrade that cannot create the new volumes after removing the old ones can leave the router unbootable.

docs.title: Check your router
docs.text:
On a router running OpenWrt:

cat /proc/mtd
  • The rootfs partition must be at least 0x08000000 (128 MiB, 512 blocks).
  • On a stock layout that partition appears as rootfs_bak / rootfs1_bak instead. If you see that, do not flash this image.

Never flash an image built for another layout

The partition table lives on the router, not in the image. An image built for a different table can brick the router.

docs.title: If your router has the stock layout
docs.text:
CleanWRT does not convert the layout. Use a layout-conversion procedure from the OpenWrt community for this device first, and only then install CleanWRT. Make sure you can reach the serial console before you start; you will need it if anything goes wrong.

Next: Recovery. Read it before you flash.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
How do I check the flash layout of my Arcadyan AW1000?

Run cat /proc/mtd on a router that runs OpenWrt. The rootfs partition must be at least 0x08000000 (128 MiB). If it shows up as rootfs_bak instead, you have the stock layout, so do not flash this image.

Why does OpenWrt not fit on the stock AW1000 flash layout?

The stock rootfs partition leaves 316 erase blocks for UBI volumes, while a CleanWRT image needs over 500 (the current release measures 514). The build checks this and fails if the image does not fit the layout it targets.

Can I flash CleanWRT if my AW1000 has the stock layout?

No. CleanWRT does not convert the layout. Use a layout-conversion procedure from the OpenWrt community first, make sure you can reach the serial console, and only then install.

docs.title: Recovery and unbrick
docs.text:
Read this page before you flash. The AW1000 has a single NAND layout with no A/B fallback partition. A bad write to the kernel or rootfs partitions leaves you at the bootloader, and recovery needs the serial console.

Pick the situation that matches yours:

Situation Go to the router boots, but LuCI or SSH is unreachable or misconfigured Failsafe mode boot loop, the LEDs stop early, or a sysupgrade was interrupted Bootloader recovery the serial console shows nothing at all U-Boot is broken

docs.title: Failsafe mode
docs.text:
Use it when the router boots but you cannot reach it.

  1. Set your computer's network card to 192.168.1.x (for example 192.168.1.10) and connect to a LAN port with Ethernet.
  2. Power-cycle the router. When the boot LED starts blinking, press the reset button a few times; failsafe starts if a press is registered during boot.

  3. The router comes up at 192.168.1.1 with SSH and no root password.

    ssh root@192.168.1.1
mount_root          # mount the overlay so you can edit your config
firstboot && reboot # factory reset (destroys your configuration)
# or fix the specific file under /overlay/upper/... and then: reboot

Failsafe works only over Ethernet. It does not work over Wi-Fi or the 5G modem.

docs.title: Bootloader level recovery (U-Boot alive)
docs.text:
Symptoms: boot loop, the LED stops early, or you interrupted a sysupgrade.

  1. Connect the UART and interrupt U-Boot.
  2. Boot an initramfs image over TFTP (tftpboot then bootm, see Installation). Nothing is written to flash, so this works even with a corrupt rootfs.
  3. From the live RAM system, run sysupgrade -v with a full *-sysupgrade.bin.

docs.title: U-Boot itself is broken
docs.text: If the bootloader does not answer on the UART (no prompt, no countdown), recovery means reprogramming the NAND chip externally, with a programmer clipped onto the chip or after removing it. That is the real brick wall. It is why you should double-check the MTD layout and the image name before every flash.

docs.title: What sysupgrade keeps
docs.text:
Mode Result default (keep settings) /etc/config/* and the overlay survive: passwords, Wi-Fi keys and enabled services carry across releases sysupgrade -n clean slate: no root password, Wi-Fi back to the default key CleanWRT#40, every opt-in service back to disabled

Upgrades do not re-run first-boot scripts

On a keep-settings upgrade, fixes to defaults apply only to settings that are still at their default. When a release note mentions a default-credential fix, do a sysupgrade -n or rotate the affected credentials by hand.

docs.title: Packages replaced by apk upgrade
docs.text: A factory reset does not restore packages that apk upgrade replaced. To get back to the state of a release, flash that release again. See Updating and pinning.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
How do I unbrick an Arcadyan AW1000?

If U-Boot still answers on the serial console, interrupt it, boot an initramfs image over TFTP (nothing is written to flash), then run sysupgrade with a full image from that live system. If U-Boot itself is dead, the NAND has to be reprogrammed with an external programmer.

How do I enter failsafe mode on the AW1000?

Connect a computer over Ethernet and set it to 192.168.1.x, power-cycle the router, and press the reset button a few times once the boot LED starts blinking. The router then comes up at 192.168.1.1 over SSH with no root password. Failsafe does not work over Wi-Fi or the 5G modem.

What happens if a sysupgrade is interrupted on the AW1000?

You may end up in a boot loop or at the bootloader. The AW1000 has a single NAND layout with no A/B fallback partition, so recovery goes through the serial console and an initramfs image.

Does a factory reset undo an apk upgrade?

No. A factory reset does not restore packages that apk upgrade replaced. Flash the release image again to get back to the state of that release.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
Images are published on the project's GitHub Releases page. Every release is built by the build workflow in the repository, from the sources pinned in the release tag.

A tag v<version> builds the images into a draft release, where they can be checked first. The release is published by hand, and that publish is also what tells this site (and the update notice in LuCI) that the version exists.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
A version looks like 25.12.5-rc1: the OpenWrt base (25.12.5) and the stage.

Stage Meaning -rc1, -rc2 ... release candidates. They are the testing series. -rc1.1 ... a fix after the candidate was published -R1, -R2 ... stable releases of the base. -R1 is the first of them. no suffix (25.12.5) reserved: a base update carries the new OpenWrt version

docs.title: What a release contains
docs.text: File What it is cleanwrt-<version>-qualcommax-ipq807x-arcadyan_aw1000-squashfs-sysupgrade.bin the permanent image, installed with sysupgrade …-initramfs-uImage.itb a boot-in-RAM image, used for the very first install from the stock firmware …-squashfs-factory.ubi the raw UBI image *.manifest every package in the image with its version profiles.json machine-readable image description (also used by the LuCI update check) sha256sums, sha256sums.cw checksums of the images and of the provenance files provenance.tar.gz the full build .config, the seed, the pinned feed list, the local package pins and the exact source commits

docs.title: Verify before you flash
docs.text:
Always check the checksum. A corrupted image is the most common cause of a bad flash.

Linux / macOSWindows (PowerShell) 
sha256sum -c sha256sums.cw --ignore-missing

Get-FileHash .\cleanwrt-*-sysupgrade.bin -Algorithm SHA256
# compare with the matching line in sha256sums.cw

Check the model too

The filename must contain arcadyan_aw1000. Never flash an image built for another device or another flash layout.

docs.title: Update notice in LuCI
docs.text: The Status → Overview page can tell you when a newer CleanWRT is published. It reads a small file on the project site, so it needs internet access. You can switch it off any time with Stop showing upgrade alerts. The check never installs anything.

docs.title: Reproducing a release
docs.text: The release tag, configs/arcadyan_aw1000.seed, feeds.conf.default, configs/local-packages.pin and patches/ are the complete input. See Build from source.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
Where can I download CleanWRT for the Arcadyan AW1000?

From the project's GitHub Releases page. Each release has the sysupgrade image, the initramfs image for a first install, a package manifest, checksums and a provenance bundle.

How do I check the checksum of the image before flashing?

On Linux or macOS run sha256sum -c sha256sums.cw --ignore-missing in the folder with the files. On Windows use Get-FileHash in PowerShell and compare the value with the matching line. A corrupted image is the most common cause of a bad flash.

What does rc1 mean in a CleanWRT version?

It is a release candidate: the testing series before a stable release. In 25.12.5-rc1, 25.12.5 is the OpenWrt base and rc1 is the first candidate. A suffix such as rc1.1 is a fix published after the candidate.

docs.title: Repositories
docs.text:
CleanWRT is built from a few small repositories, all on GitHub under Pr0Luci. The firmware repository pins the others to an exact commit.

Repository What it is Documentation cleanwrt-aw1000 the firmware: build configuration, patches, rootfs overlay, workflows and this documentation Build from source, Contributing openwrt-aw1000-voice-awvoice AWvoice: the kernel module, the phone daemon and the LuCI page for the RJ11 port AWvoice luci-app-cw-led the front-panel LED daemon and its LuCI page Front-panel LEDs luci-theme-footstrap the LuCI theme the image selects (upstream, unpatched) The Footstrap theme

docs.title: How they fit together
docs.text:
cleanwrt-aw1000  (feeds.conf.default, configs/local-packages.pin, patches/)
   ├── pins  luci-app-cw-led      → LED daemon and page
   ├── pins  luci-theme-footstrap → default theme
   ├── pins  AWvoice              → phone port
   └── pins  OpenWrt, LuCI, QModem, Passwall, 3ginfo-lite, ... (upstream feeds)

A change in one of the smaller repositories reaches the firmware only when the firmware repository moves its pin to the new commit. That is a pull request of its own, so every release is built from commits you can read.

docs.title: Where to report things
docs.text:
• A problem with the firmware, a package or these docs: an issue in cleanwrt-aw1000.
  • A problem that is clearly inside one of the other parts: an issue in that repository.
  • A mistake on a docs page: Edit this page (the pencil at the top of every page) opens it on GitHub, and a pull request fixes it.

docs.title: The Footstrap theme
docs.text: CleanWRT ships with Footstrap as its web interface. It is an ordinary LuCI theme maintained upstream as luci-theme-footstrap (Apache-2.0), pinned to one commit in configs/local-packages.pin like every other out-of-feed package here. CleanWRT changes one line of it - patches/packages/luci-theme-footstrap/0001-login-page-carries-the-image-logo.patch puts the CleanWRT logo on the login page where the theme otherwise prints the router's hostname - and nothing else: what you see is the theme as its own author publishes it, selected by files/etc/uci-defaults/96-cw-default-theme on first boot.

docs.title: What it looks like
docs.text:
• Dark by default, with light and auto modes, and a choice per browser as well as one saved on the router.
  • A top bar or a sidebar for the menu, and a narrow-screen layout below 768 px.
  • Five palettes - Footstrap, Bootstrap, 2020, Forum and Hi-Contrast - plus a free accent colour you can set by hue or by hex.
  • Frosted surfaces: cards, controls and bars each take their own colour, material (flat, acrylic or frosted), opacity and a blur amount, with a corner rounding from 0 to 20 px.
  • A wallpaper behind the pages: an SVG pattern of your own, or a photo, with the pattern's size, strength and ink and the photo's dimming all adjustable. The login page takes the same photo, and carries the CleanWRT logo above the username.
  • Density (normal, compact, large) and a content width from 1280 to 3840 px.
